# Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
## FEDS Notes
### AI Adoption and Firms' Job-Posting Behavior
#### Introduction
This note uses job postings data from Lightcast and the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey to investigate the relationship between AI adoption and firms' job-posting behavior. We find that thus far, there is no evidence of a reduction in job postings for industries or firms which have higher levels of AI adoption. The overall slowdown in national job postings following the pandemic recovery does not appear to be driven (even modestly) by AI.
#### Literature Review
Research on the effect of AI on employment and wages varies. Hartley et al. (2024) find that generative AI exposure has little or no significant effect on total jobs or job postings, though AI-exposed occupations have statistically significant wage gains. Similarly, Acemoglu et al.
(2022) observe no relationship between AI exposure and overall employment or wages at the industry- or occupation-level, but do find that AI-exposed establishments reduced hiring in non-AI positions. Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen (2025) find entry-level employment declines in occupations where AI primarily automates work, but stable or growing employment for more experienced workers in the same occupations, and for workers in less AI-exposed fields.

# AI Exposure Isn’t Squeezing Advertised Pay in the US — It’s Boosting It
One of the most common AI-fueled worries is that the technology will hollow out knowledge work and drag down pay for those jobs that remain. But almost four years after the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, US job postings data tell a different story. Advertised wages in the occupations most exposed to AI aren’t falling behind. Instead, they’re growing faster than in less-exposed jobs.
## AI-exposed roles have pulled ahead on pay
Since 2021, advertised pay in the most AI-exposed occupations has climbed by about 46% (versus 25% in the least-exposed). Pay in more- and less-exposed occupations tracked closely for the first year after ChatGPT launched.
## How do the trends differ by seniority?
Splitting the same index by the seniority level stated in the posting shows the premium widens as you move up the job hierarchy. At the senior level, the gap is largest and opens earliest: More-exposed pay grew 45% from its 2021 level by mid-2026, compared with 28% for less-exposed pay, a gap of about 17 points.
It’s important to note that because we measure advertised pay in posted jobs, some of the rise reflects a shift toward fewer, more senior postings. That shift is larger in more AI-exposed work. In the most-exposed occupations, the entry-level share of postings fell from 29% to 10% between 2021 and 2026, while the senior share rose from 22% to 47%.

## Geunyong Park

National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

Date Written: May 10, 2026

### Abstract

This paper examines whether mandated pay ratio disclosure induces firms to restructure their workforce composition. Under the Dodd-Frank Act, U.S. publicly traded firms were required beginning in 2018 to disclose the ratio of CEO annual total compensation to the median employee's pay. Using a continuous difference-indifferences design that exploits cross-sectional variation in firms' initial disclosure pay ratios, I analyze online job posting data from Lightcast for a sample of publicly traded firms over 2013-2023. Firms with one standard deviation higher pay ratios post 7.8% less job ads after the disclosure. The reduction in job postings entails a substantial restructuring of hiring: They post significantly more job ads with wage disclosure and a work-from-home option, while reducing job ads for low-education and junior positions. These shifts in hiring composition are accompanied by a documented rise in median employee compensation and a decline in overall employment. The findings indicate that pay ratio disclosure induces firms to manage the reported figure through workforce composition rather than through genuine wage increases, paradoxically reducing job opportunities for the low-wage workers the mandate was designed to protect.

# Financial Fraud Exposure and Ethics-Related Value Signaling in Recruitment

## Abstract

Recruitment strategy has been a central topic of human resource management (HRM) research, yet little is known about how firms communicate values when their legitimacy is under threat. Corporate misconduct exposure presents a unique dilemma: firms must attract talent while facing job seekers’ heightened skepticism. In such moments, what values firms choose to highlight or withhold in recruitment messaging becomes especially consequential. Drawing on reactive impression management and expectancy violation theory, we examine how financial fraud exposure influences firms’ ethics-related value signaling in job advertisements. We theorize that firms will avoid emphasizing ethics after financial fraud exposure in job advertisements because doing so could increase perceived inconsistencies between espoused values and recent behavior. This tendency is amplified when scrutiny is greater, such as under extensive media coverage and among Best Places to Work (BPTW) firms. Analyzing 88,250 accounting-related job postings from U.S. public firms between 2015 and 2022 provides strong evidence that firms reduce ethics-related value disclosures after fraud exposure. Our findings contribute to HRM research by shedding light on how corporate recruitment strategies evolve following the exposure of corporate misconduct.

## Abstract

We study the impact of AI on labor markets using establishment-level data on vacancies with detailed occupation and skill information comprising the near-universe of online vacancies in the US from 2010 onwards. exa-lite.snippet:
## Abstract

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to transform work, but less is known about how firms reorganize labor demand as the technology diffuses. Existing research has largely focused on which occupations are exposed to AI or whether exposed jobs decline. We extend this debate by examining whether firms adjust by changing where they hire, what jobs contain, or both. Using a nationwide dataset of job postings in the United States, covering all sectors of the economy, we construct a dynamic, posting-level measure of generative AI exposure with a two-stage large language model pipeline. The pipeline identifies the tasks described in each posting and classifies the extent to which generative AI can perform or assist them. We then decompose changes in aggregate exposure into two margins: reallocation of demand across jobs and redesign of tasks within jobs. We document three main findings. First, generative AI exposure is dynamic rather than fixed, changing substantially over time. Second, labor demand adjusts through both margins. Hiring reallocation explains the largest share of the aggregate decline in exposure, accounting for 52% on average, while within-job redesign becomes increasingly important, accounting for 39.5%. A complementary Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition shows that shifts in occupational composition account for about 90% of the exposure change attributable to observable job characteristics. Third, adjustment differs across the job ladder. Senior jobs adjust earlier and mainly through reallocation, whereas junior jobs adjust through a broader mix of reallocation, redesign, and their interaction. These findings suggest that labor market adjustment to generative AI is a process of organizational reconfiguration, in which firms reshape both hiring demand and the task architecture of work.

The debate on whether AI is negatively affecting entry-level graduate jobs is everywhere, with the two sides of the debate firmly sticking to opposing arguments. On the one side, doomsayers believe that [AI is replacing large swaths](https://www.reveliolabs.com/news/ai-and-work/is-ai-just-a-scapegoat-for-layoffs) of entry-level roles, quoting tech CEOs on grand statements about AI and their future HR strategies. jina.snippet:
Artificial intelligence is often portrayed as a job killer, but new research tracking AI adoption from 2010 to 2023 paints a more nuanced picture: AI’s impact is often on specific tasks within jobs rather than on whole occupations.

A[new study](https://www.nber.org/papers/w33509) co-authored by MIT Sloan associate professor found that when AI can perform most of the tasks that make up a particular job, the share of people in that role within a company falls by about 14%.

But when AI’s impact is concentrated in just a few tasks within a role — leaving other responsibilities untouched — employment in that role can grow. The reason? With some of their tasks automated, workers can focus on activities where AI is less capable, such as critical thinking or coming up with new ideas.

keenable.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
keenable.snippet: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms’ stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm’s exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms’ mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.

keenable.title: AI Exposure and the Changing Responsibilities in Job Postings
keenable.snippet: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace has raised questions about how employer demand for different work activities is changing. We examine how the prevalence and content of work activities in online job postings change in association with activity-level measures of AI exposure, derived from Copilot and Claude usage. To enable systematic comparisons, we develop a pipeline that extracts the responsibilities from job advertisements and maps them onto O*NET's standardized taxonomy of Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). We then apply this approach to 50,000 job advertisements from 33 firms between 2023 and 2025. From this analysis, we first find that explicit mentions of AI increased by 66%, although much of this growth occurs outside descriptions of the actual work activities associated with a job. Looking specifically at the advertised job responsibilities, activities with greater AI exposure tend to decline in advertised prevalence, but only mildly as a share of the total number of responsibilities. At the same time, more AI-exposed work activities increasingly are associated with explicitly AI-related responsibilities, suggesting that employers are looking to hire people who can perform these responsibilities with AI.

keenable.title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor‑Market Effects of AI?
keenable.snippet:
In this post, we examine whether early evidence of AI’s effect on the labor market appears in firms’ job postings. We combine an occupational measure of AI exposure with detailed U.S. job-posting data from Lightcast, which aggregates listings from company career pages, national and local job boards, and job-listing aggregators. Using this data, we test whether postings for AI-exposed occupations declined disproportionately since the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. We find that, while overall hiring has slowed since then, the evidence from job postings provides little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand.
#### Measuring a Job’s Exposure to AI
To measure how exposed different jobs are to AI, we use a [task-level AI exposure metric developed by Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts) that combines detailed task descriptions from [O*NET](https://www.onetcenter.org/database.html) with observed AI usage. O*NET breaks each occupation into a set of specific activities that workers regularly perform. For example, a copywriter may edit or rewrite marketing text, while a web developer may write supporting code for websites and web applications. The Anthropic measure evaluates each task and assigns it an AI exposure score based on three factors: whether the task could theoretically be mostly completed by AI; whether the task actually appears in a sample of AI usage data; and whether AI is used to [automate the task rather than augment it](https://assets.anthropic.com/m/2e23255f1e84ca97/original/Economic_Tasks_AI_Paper.pdf).

To examine whether AI is affecting labor demand, we conduct an event study that compares how job postings evolve for occupations with relatively high versus low AI exposure around the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Here, we define high-exposure occupations as those with an AI exposure of at least 0.2; the results are similar under alternative cutoff values.

keenable-realtime.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
keenable-realtime.snippet: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms’ stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm’s exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms’ mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.

Abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace has raised questions about how employer demand for different work activities is changing. Abstract
We study whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) constitutes a form of seniority-biased technological change, disproportionately affecting junior relative to senior workers. Using U.S. résumé and job posting data covering nearly 62 million workers in 285,000 firms (2015-2025), we track within-firm employment dynamics by seniority.
We identify AI adoption through a text-analysis approach that flags postings for dedicated “AI integrator” roles, signaling active implementation of generative AI. Difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimates show that, beginning in 2023Q1, junior employment in adopting firms declined sharply relative to non-adopters, while senior employment continued to rise.

Heterogeneity by education reveals a U-shaped pattern: mid-tier graduates see the largest declines, while elite and low-tier graduates are less affected. Overall, the results provide early evidence of a seniority-biased impact of AI adoption and its mechanisms.

increased in hiring contexts, especially for computing jobs, there is still

## **Job postings show early signs of AI automation impact**

September 01, 2026

Texas firms are increasingly integrating generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into their business processes. Two-thirds of firms surveyed in the May 2026 Texas Business Outlook Survey reported using AI, up from 40 percent two years prior.

The rapid adoption of GenAI tools, which iteratively refine their capabilities based on tasks assigned, raises concerns of labor market disruption as the new technology automates work humans previously performed. While it increases worker productivity, it may also reduce the demand for certain types of labor.

A new analysis, using data from millions of online job postings, shows GenAI is reshaping labor demand in Texas. We measure the exposure of individual occupations to automation based on observed capabilities of GenAI tools to perform particular tasks.

After the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, job openings fell for occupations whose tasks are automatable by GenAI. Surviving incumbent firms posted fewer openings and shifted the composition of their job posts away from more AI-exposed occupations.

ultimate.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
ultimate.snippet: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms’ stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm’s exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms’ mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.

ultimate.title: AI Exposure and the Changing Responsibilities in Job Postings
ultimate.snippet: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace has raised questions about how employer demand for different work activities is changing. We examine how the prevalence and content of work activities in online job postings change in association with activity-level measures of AI exposure, derived from Copilot and Claude usage. To enable systematic comparisons, we develop a pipeline that extracts the responsibilities from job advertisements and maps them onto O*NET's standardized taxonomy of Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). We then apply this approach to 50,000 job advertisements from 33 firms between 2023 and 2025. From this analysis, we first find that explicit mentions of AI increased by 66%, although much of this growth occurs outside descriptions of the actual work activities associated with a job. Looking specifically at the advertised job responsibilities, activities with greater AI exposure tend to decline in advertised prevalence, but only mildly as a share of the total number of responsibilities. At the same time, more AI-exposed work activities increasingly are associated with explicitly AI-related responsibilities, suggesting that employers are looking to hire people who can perform these responsibilities with AI.

ultimate.title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor‑Market Effects of AI?
ultimate.snippet:
In this post, we examine whether early evidence of AI’s effect on the labor market appears in firms’ job postings. We combine an occupational measure of AI exposure with detailed U.S. job-posting data from Lightcast, which aggregates listings from company career pages, national and local job boards, and job-listing aggregators. Using this data, we test whether postings for AI-exposed occupations declined disproportionately since the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. We find that, while overall hiring has slowed since then, the evidence from job postings provides little indication of a distinct AI-driven decline in labor demand.
#### Measuring a Job’s Exposure to AI
To measure how exposed different jobs are to AI, we use a [task-level AI exposure metric developed by Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts) that combines detailed task descriptions from [O*NET](https://www.onetcenter.org/database.html) with observed AI usage. O*NET breaks each occupation into a set of specific activities that workers regularly perform. For example, a copywriter may edit or rewrite marketing text, while a web developer may write supporting code for websites and web applications. The Anthropic measure evaluates each task and assigns it an AI exposure score based on three factors: whether the task could theoretically be mostly completed by AI; whether the task actually appears in a sample of AI usage data; and whether AI is used to [automate the task rather than augment it](https://assets.anthropic.com/m/2e23255f1e84ca97/original/Economic_Tasks_AI_Paper.pdf).

To examine whether AI is affecting labor demand, we conduct an event study that compares how job postings evolve for occupations with relatively high versus low AI exposure around the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Here, we define high-exposure occupations as those with an AI exposure of at least 0.2; the results are similar under alternative cutoff values.

ultimate.title: Generative AI and the Reorganization of Labor Demand
ultimate.snippet: We extend this debate by examining whether firms adjust by changing where they hire, what jobs contain, or both. Using a nationwide dataset of job postings in the United States, covering all sectors of the economy, we construct a dynamic, posting-level measure of generative AI exposure with a two-stage large language model pipeline. The pipeline identifies the tasks described in each posting and classifies the extent to which generative AI can perform or assist them. We then decompose changes in aggregate exposure into two margins: reallocation of demand across jobs and redesign of tasks within jobs. We document three main findings. First, generative AI exposure is dynamic rather than fixed, changing substantially over time. Second, labor demand adjusts through both margins. Hiring reallocation explains the largest share of the aggregate decline in exposure, accounting for 52% on average, while within-job redesign becomes increasingly important, accounting for 39.5%. A complementary Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition shows that shifts in occupational composition account for about 90% of the exposure change attributable to observable job characteristics. Third, adjustment differs across the job ladder. Senior jobs adjust earlier and mainly through reallocation, whereas junior jobs adjust through a broader mix of reallocation, redesign, and their interaction.

Marketing AI Exposure: Applicability Breadth, Substitution Depth, and Job Outcomes
As AI reshapes organizational work, its overlap with marketing responsibilities raises questions
about its impact on marketing jobs. This research introduces Marketing AI Exposure as a two-
dimensional construct comprising AI applicability breadth and AI substitution depth.
Applicability breadth captures the range of AI technologies relevant to a job’s task portfolio,
whereas substitution depth captures the extent to which AI can perform those tasks. Using
dependency parsing to extract verb-noun pairs from approximately 4.86 million marketing job
postings and 1.3 million AI patents, we construct job posting-level measures of both dimensions.
Regression analyses show that breadth is associated with higher hiring but lower wages, whereas
depth is associated with lower hiring and lower wages. Jobs high on both dimensions show the
strongest wage compression, but not uniform hiring contraction, underscoring the value of
distinguishing AI availability from task coverage. The research also shows that marketing skills

ultimate.title: AI Exposure and the Changing Responsibilities in Job Postings
ultimate.snippet: > Abstract:The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace has raised questions about how employer demand for different work activities is changing. We examine how the prevalence and content of work activities in online job postings change in association with activity-level measures of AI exposure, derived from Copilot and Claude usage. To enable systematic comparisons, we develop a pipeline that extracts the responsibilities from job advertisements and maps them onto O*NET's standardized taxonomy of Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs). We then apply this approach to 50,000 job advertisements from 33 firms between 2023 and 2025. From this analysis, we first find that explicit mentions of AI increased by 66%, although much of this growth occurs outside descriptions of the actual work activities associated with a job. Looking specifically at the advertised job responsibilities, activities with greater AI exposure tend to decline in advertised prevalence, but only mildly as a share of the total number of responsibilities. At the same time, more AI-exposed work activities increasingly are associated with explicitly AI-related responsibilities, suggesting that employers are looking to hire people who can perform these responsibilities with AI.
